About this citation

The modern title is a convention; the Greek means 'to himself'. Section numbering differs between editions, so a book-and-section locator should name the edition it follows.

### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“Once in a lifetime, everything must be doubted.”

Latin

“Semel in vita de omnibus, quantum fieri potest, esse dubitandum.”

“Once in a life, as far as possible, everything must be doubted.” The words “once in a lifetime” carry the whole method: this is a single act of demolition, not a standing policy.

### Attribution notes

The sentence is Descartes' statement of the method of the first Meditation. It is routinely recited as a general endorsement of scepticism, which inverts it: Descartes doubts once in order to find something that cannot be doubted, and the point of the exercise is the foundation he reaches at the end of the second Meditation.

#### About René Descartes

René Descartes (1596–1650) was a French mathematician and philosopher who helped launch early modern rationalism. Educated by Jesuits, he traveled as a soldier and settled for long periods in the Dutch Republic.

### How to read this passage

Epistemology asks whether knowledge is justified true belief, reliable tracking of the world, or something else; it also asks how perception, testimony, memory, and reason contribute. This passage enters that discussion through knowledge, method, truth.
